extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of literature, theatre, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: The page gives a theoretical analysis of what makes situations comic in comedy and theatrical writing, identifying archetypal mechanical diagrams (types) and methods (repetition, inversion, interference) the comic author can use. Useful for analyzing or constructing comic scenes across plays and light comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion of life combined with impression of mechanical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any arrangement of acts and events is comic which gives us, in a single combination, the illusion of life and the distinct impression of a mechanical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as the fundamental law: comedy introduces mechanism into outward forms of life. Examples throughout the chapter instantiate how otherwise-living behavior, when seen as mechanical or automatic, becomes laughable. Use this as the primary test for whether a scene is comic: does it simultaneously suggest vitality and mechanical automatism?

rubrics_metrics.name: Jack-in-the-box (mechanical repetition / spring imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: A struggle between two stubborn elements, one simply mechanical and the other treating it as a plaything; the image of a spring that is bent, released, and bent again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Punch and Judy (policeman repeatedly felled then springs up), the repeated 'Monsieur Purgon!' beats in Le Malade Imaginaire, and scenes where a character is pushed back and reappears like a man in a box (Sganarelle and Pancrace). This type relies on visible rhythm/tempo and repeated mechanical return; it often symbolizes a repressed feeling that repeatedly springs forth while an idea represses it anew. Writers can achieve comic effect by staging a regular, mechanical repetition that contrasts with the expected living continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-repetition as sign of inner mechanical struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: The repetition of a word or phrase is not laughable in itself; it makes us laugh because it symbolises a special play of moral elements — a repressed feeling which goes off like a spring, and an idea that delights in repressing the feeling anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dorine's repeated 'Et Tartuffe?' in Tartuffe, Alceste's repeated 'I don't say that!' in Molière. Use word-repetition to signal an internal oscillation (e.g., between candor and politeness) whose mechanical renewal grows the comic tension until release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of situations (situational recurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation — a combination of circumstances — which recurs several times in its original form and thus contrasts with the changing stream of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is laughable in proportion as the repeated scene is complex and naturally introduced. Examples: Molière's École des femmes (same incident in three tempi), George Dandin's three-tempo effect, and contemporary light comedies that reproduce identical incidents under ever-fresh circumstances. Authors may repeat entire episodes across acts or have different character-groups (masters/servants) repeat a scene in another key; success depends on reconciling naturalness with mathematical order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack (character as puppet manipulated by another)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character who thinks he speaks and acts freely but, from a certain standpoint, appears a mere toy in the hands of another who pulls the strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scapin manipulating Géronte and Argante; Panurge asking Tom, Dick, and Harry whether he ought to marry (vacillation between personified opposing decisions). Comic authors should personify the two contrary decisions or provide actors/spectators to hold the strings; the spectator may side with the knave/manipulator. The image converts apparent freedom into visible mechanism, producing comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball (arithmetical progression / accumulating chain reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: An effect which grows by arithmetical progression: a small, initially insignificant cause evolves inevitably into an unexpectedly large result through a necessary concatenation of consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rolling snow-ball, toy soldiers toppling chain, house of cards collapsing, a lost letter that 'rolls up' ever more serious incidents, Labiche's straw hat (keeps slipping away), plays where repeated mishaps escalate until final collapse. This mechanism can be rectilinear or circular (more laughable when circular and reversible). Use cumulative cause-effect chains to create accelerating comic momentum and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circularity / reversibility (return-to-start and futile effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanical combination that is reversible or circular, so that a great deal of activity brings one unwittingly back to the starting-point — an effort that encounters a void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comedies where characters go through many complications only to return to their original state (marriage/divorce leading back to same spouse), Labiche's plays where the pursued object turns out absent/consumed. The idea echoes Spencer/Kant 'expectation ending in nothing' but Bergson warns that lack of proportion alone is not sufficient; the comic arises when circularity reveals a mechanical arrangement or absent-mindedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (topsyturvydom / robber robbed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing the situation or inverting roles produces comedy: a trap set by a character in which he is the first to be caught; a villain who becomes victim of his own villainy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: double rescue in Le Voyage de M. Perrichon, Lawyer Pathelin's client outwitting the lawyer, the 'robber robbed' stock type. Inversion often becomes a classical comic model that endows superficially unrelated mishaps with comic overtones by association— even an allusion to such a mishap can suffice to produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series / equivocal situations
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is comic when it simultaneously belongs to two altogether independent series of events and can be interpreted in two entirely different meanings at the same time — an equivocal situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encompasses misunderstandings, double-entendre scenarios, and any case where two independent frames of reference overlap to produce ambiguity. The term 'interference' is used analogously to optics (partial superposition and neutralisation). Equivocal situations are highly varied on the stage and often underpin farce and situational comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as exposure of absent-mindedness; laughter as social corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is that side of a person which reveals his likeness to a thing — the impression of mechanism, automatism, or movement without life — an individual or collective imperfection signaling 'absent-mindedness' in life or events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson frames laughter as a social gesture that singles out and represses this particular absent-mindedness. Thus, beyond devices and plot-types, the author can aim to make characters' inelasticity, rigidity, or inattentiveness visible to provoke laughter; comedy thereby performs a corrective social function. This theoretical criterion ties the other methods (repetition, inversion, interference) to a philosophical explanation of why they are laughable.
